'''Chester Theodore Raymo Jr.''' (September 17, 1936 – January 25, 2026) was an American writer, educator and naturalist. He was professor emeritus of physics at [[Stonehill College]], in [[Easton, Massachusetts]]. His weekly newspaper column "Science Musings" appeared in the ''[[Boston Globe]]'' for twenty years from 1983 to 2003, now collected and extended with his further writings on his personal website. Raymo espoused his [[religious naturalism]] in ''When God is Gone Everything is Holy – The Making of a Religious Naturalist'' and frequently in his blog. He said: "I attend to this infinitely mysterious world with reverence, awe, thanksgiving, praise. All religious qualities."<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.stonehill.edu/x16569.xml|title= Stonehill College|publisher= stonehill.edu|accessdate= 2011-03-21|url-status= dead|archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20110720050818/http://www.stonehill.edu/x16569.xml|archivedate= July 20, 2011|df= mdy-all}}</ref>

Raymo was a contributor to ''The Notre Dame Magazine''<ref>{{cite web |url=http://magazine.nd.edu/news/14932-let-me-begin-this-celebration-of-life/|title= to The Notre Dame Magazine |publisher= magazine.nd.edu|accessdate= 2011-03-18}}</ref> and ''Scientific American''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/author.cfm?id=159
|title=Scientific American |publisher=scientificamerican.com|accessdate= February 3, 2010}}</ref>

Raymo's most famous book is the novel entitled ''The Dork of Cork'', which was made into the feature-length film ''[[Frankie Starlight]]''. He is also the author of ''Walking Zero'', a scientific and historical account of his wanderings along the [[Prime Meridian]] in Great Britain. He was the recipient of the 1998 [[Lannan Literary Awards|Lannan Literary Award]] for his non-fiction work.

Raymo espoused a scientific skepticism for his beliefs:
{{Blockquote|For the Religious Naturalist, darkness and silence are not the paradox, they are the resolution. The [[Apophatic theology|apophatic]] tradition ends in effective negation (God is not this, God is not that, God is not). Not only do we fall silent in the face of the Word, the Word itself dissolves into silence. We too walk a fine line; not between skepticism and faith, but between skepticism and cynicism. We try to stay firmly on the side of skepticism, open to whatever winds of wisdom blow our way, and as for knowledge of the world, we cherish the scientific way of knowing—tentative, partial, evolving.<ref>Chet Raymo's blog January 22, 2013</ref>}}

Raymo died on January 25, 2026, at the age of 89.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Chester T. "Chet" Raymo Jr.|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/name/chester-raymo-obituary?id=60674202|website=Legacy|access-date=2026-01-31}}</ref>
